title: First-order kinetics and half-life
subtitle: Constant exponential decay independent of starting concentration

learn.prompt: A therapeutic compound breaks down via first-order kinetics with a half-life of 4 hours. If a patient takes a 100 mg dose, how much remains active after 8 hours?
learn.hint: Calculate the number of half-lives: 8 hours / 4 hours = 2 half-lives. Each half-life cuts the amount in half.
learn.explanation: After 4 hours (1 half-life), 50 mg remains. After 8 hours (2 half-lives), 25 mg remains: 100 x (1/2)^2 = 25 mg.

misconceptionMap.b: 50 mg remains after only 4 hours (1 half-life).
misconceptionMap.d: Exponential decay approaches zero asymptotically; it does not reach zero in 2 half-lives.

learn.prompt: A reactant sample has a half-life of 20 minutes. Starting with 80 mg, at what elapsed time will exactly 20 mg remain?
learn.hint: 80 mg -> 40 mg (1st half-life) -> 20 mg (2nd half-life). Two half-lives of 20 min each.
learn.explanation: The quantity halves twice to drop from 80 mg to 20 mg. Two half-lives equal 2 x 20 min = 40 min.

check.prompt: What distinctive characteristic defines a first-order chemical reaction compared to zero- or second-order reactions?
check.hint: Look at the formula t_1/2 = ln(2) / k. Does [A] appear anywhere in it?
check.explanation: Because t_1/2 = ln(2) / k, the half-life of a first-order reaction is completely constant and independent of the initial reactant concentration.

options.label: Its half-life is constant and independent of starting concentration
Its reaction rate is completely constant over time
Its half-life doubles as the reactant is consumed
It requires a catalyst to proceed

misconceptionMap.b: Constant reaction rate defines a zero-order reaction (Rate = k).
misconceptionMap.c: Half-life increasing as concentration drops is characteristic of second-order reactions (t_1/2 = 1/(k[A]0)).
misconceptionMap.d: Catalysts alter activation energy, but any reaction order can be catalyzed or uncatalyzed.

check.prompt: A chemical reactant with a half-life of 15 minutes begins with a mass of 64 mg. How much remains after 45 minutes?
check.explanation: 45 minutes represents 3 half-lives. Halving 64 mg three times gives 64 -> 32 -> 16 -> 8 mg.

misconceptionMap.c: That subtracts 64/3 linearly instead of halving exponentially.
misconceptionMap.d: 4 mg would be after 4 half-lives (60 min).

takeaway.title: First-order half-life is an invariant of the reaction
takeaway.body: Because t_1/2 = ln(2) / k, every first-order process takes the exact same amount of time to halve its remaining material, whether starting at 1000 moles or 1 mole. This invariant is the foundation of radiocarbon dating and pharmacokinetics.
